facts.text: Writer-director Larry Cohen first wrote this story around 1967 as a script called The Cutting Room. It sat unmade for roughly 17 years.
Writer-director Larry Cohen once hoped to option his script Daddy's Gone A-Hunting to Alfred Hitchcock. Universal instead hired Mark Robson to direct it in 1969.
Larry Cohen called the film his "revenge on big budget directors." His washed-up filmmaker Christopher Neville is a director with a couple of flops who can't get hired anymore.
Star Eric Bogosian's first screen appearance was Born in Flames (1983), a zero-budget feminist sci-fi indie. He played a TV technician forced at gunpoint to air a tape. Kathryn Bigelow is also in it.
Cohen's rule on set: "I always have a fight the first day, with somebody." Once you establish who's in charge, he said, they never bother you again. That day it was star Eric Bogosian.
Several scenes in Larry Cohen's film were shot guerrilla-style on New York streets without official permits, including sequences outside Radio City Music Hall.
Neville's wild loft, with its indoor pool and stained glass, was artist Lowell Nesbitt's real studio. The building had been covered by the New York Times, Vogue and Architectural Digest.
The loft used as Neville's home was a 12,500-square-foot 1858 building in Manhattan that had been a police stable. Artist Lowell Nesbitt's indoor pool was capped by city rules at four feet deep.
Larry Cohen recalled that his leads Zoë Lund, Eric Bogosian and Brad Rijn were "all highly offbeat people who lived in strange basements, had no money, and were highly talented."
Zoë Lund's voice as Andrea was dubbed by another actress, which Lund resented. She said playing two roles was "a little like Vertigo."
Zoë Lund's only major earlier role was the mute avenger in Abel Ferrara's Ms. 45 (1981). Cohen cast her in the double lead after seeing it.
Eric Bogosian wrote and starred in the 1988 film Talk Radio, a play of his that was a Pulitzer finalist. He won the Silver Bear for Best Actor at Berlin for it.
Lund's heroin use was known at the time. Cohen said it caused no trouble on this shoot: "Nothing manifested itself during the picture."
Larry Cohen says he shoots new scenes on the fly and that nobody supervises him: "No one looks at my dailies or my script!"
Cohen shot this and Perfect Strangers (1984) back to back in New York, sharing cast members like Brad Rijn and Kevin O'Connor. Cohen's Special Effects took about 20 days.
Cohen's "revenge on big budget directors" had a personal angle: he was fired from the 1981 Armand Assante thriller I, the Jury for going over budget.
The Schlock Pit's review says the film takes aim at Star 80, the movie that cashed in on the real-life murder of Playmate Dorothy Stratten.
Film critic Adrian Martin says the storyline of Detective Philip Delroy (Kevin O'Connor) was added late in shooting, and that it shows in the finished film.
Cohen said this was one of the lowest budgets of his career. He still believed it had some of his best production values.
Cohen loved working fast: he once directed Hell Up in Harlem and It's Alive at the same time, shooting It's Alive on weekdays and Hell Up in Harlem on weekends.
Neville is reportedly modeled on Michael Cimino and Peter Bogdanovich. Both suffered very public career slides in the early 1980s after expensive flops.
On the Blu-ray commentary, Larry Cohen brings up Brian De Palma's Hitchcock homage Obsession (1976) as a point of comparison for his own film.
It was released in the same year as Brian De Palma's Body Double, another Hitchcock-flavored thriller about filmmaking and voyeurism. Special Effects is often seen as its scrappier, cheaper cousin.
The film played theaters only in Minneapolis, via New Line Cinema, on November 30, 1984. Scholar Tony Williams says it "never got proper theatrical distribution and went straight to video."
Critic Adrian Martin compares Larry Cohen to Samuel Fuller: both make films packed with striking ideas, delivered in an uneven, hit-and-miss way.
Film scholars Xavier Mendik and Steven Jay Schneider say the film uses self-reflexive techniques usually associated with underground cinema. They place it in Cohen's tradition of "guerrilla cinema."
Eric Bogosian later played Gil Eavis on HBO's Succession and Arno in the Safdie brothers' Uncut Gems (2019).
Brad Rijn (Keefe) was a Cohen regular in the 1980s. He appeared in this, Perfect Strangers, and The Stuff.
Opinions differ on Michael D. Minard's synth score: Filmhounds called it "a fantastic and very overlooked synth score."
Blu-ray.com's review says the film's synth score feels like an imitation of Jan Hammer's Miami Vice music. Zoë Lund herself appeared in Miami Vice in 1984.
Before the movies, Larry Cohen created TV series including Branded and The Invaders. He was removed from creative control of Branded after one year.
Kevin O'Connor (Detective Delroy) is best known for playing Humphrey Bogart in the 1980 TV movie Bogie. He also starred in Let's Scare Jessica to Death (1971).
The film has a cult afterlife: it is referenced in War on Everyone (2017), Director's Cut (2016) and Adjust Your Tracking (2013), and spoofed in Housewife Alien vs. Gay Zombie (2020).
The UK video release lost about 30 seconds to the BBFC (the British film censors). The cuts hit two strangulations and much of a scene of a murder being watched on film.
Kevin O'Connor (Detective Delroy) won two Drama Desk Awards and an Obie on stage. He died on June 22, 1991, at age 56.
Adrian Martin wrote that the film is "ultimately, a film for Cohen aficionados," who can overlook the holes in it.
Walter Goodman of The New York Times wrote that "coherence is not the strong point here." AllMovie's Donald Guarisco called it Cohen at his "most conceptually audacious."
Cohen later wrote Phone Booth (2002) and Cellular (2004). Both are single-location gimmick thrillers sold as spec scripts, with Phone Booth going for a mid-six-figure sum.
